content: Acute diarrhoea is a significant cause of illness and death among children in low-income countries. Glucose-based oral rehydration solutions (ORS) are commonly used to replace fluids and prevent dehydration caused by acute diarrhoea. Since 2004, the World Health Organization (WHO) has recommended using ORS with an osmolarity of less than 270 mOsm/L (ORS ≤ 270) instead of formulations with osmolarity greater than 310 mOsm/L (ORS ≥ 310). Polymer-based ORS, which is made using substances like rice or wheat, releases glucose more slowly and may offer advantages over glucose-based ORS. The objective of this study was to compare the effectiveness of polymer-based ORS with glucose-based ORS in treating acute watery diarrhoea. Researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases and sources up to September 5, 2016, including MEDLINE, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Library. They also contacted experts, organizations, and pharmaceutical companies to identify relevant studies. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving individuals with acute watery diarrhoea (both cholera-associated and non-cholera-associated) were included if they compared polymer-based ORS with glucose-based ORS containing identical electrolyte compositions. A total of 35 trials involving 4284 participants met the inclusion criteria. Among these, 28 trials focused exclusively on children, five included adults, and two included both adults and children. Polymer-based ORS versus glucose-based ORS (osmolarity ≤ 270): Eight trials involving 752 participants compared polymer-based ORS with glucose-based ORS at ≤ 270 mOsm/L. Seven of these trials used rice as the polymer source. Polymer-based ORS may reduce the average stool output in the first 24 hours by 24 mL/kg (mean difference [MD] −24.60 mL/kg, 95% confidence interval [CI] −40.69 to −8.51; one trial, 99 participants; low-quality evidence). The average duration of diarrhoea may be shortened by approximately eight hours (MD −8.24 hours, 95% CI −13.17 to −3.30; five trials, 364 participants; low-quality evidence). However, there was significant variability in the results. Limited evidence from a small number of trials showed no significant difference in the risk of requiring unscheduled intravenous fluid (relative risk [RR] 0.66, 95% CI 0.43 to 1.02; four trials, 376 participants; very low-quality evidence), vomiting (very low-quality evidence), or hyponatraemia (very low-quality evidence). Polymer-based ORS versus glucose-based ORS (osmolarity ≥ 310): Twenty-seven trials involving 3532 participants compared polymer-based ORS with glucose-based ORS at ≥ 310 mOsm/L, using various types of polymers. Polymer-based ORS may reduce total stool output in the first 24 hours by approximately 65 mL/kg (MD −65.47 mL/kg, 95% CI −83.92 to −47.03; 16 trials, 1483 participants; low-quality evidence). The duration of diarrhoea may be reduced by about eight hours (MD −8.57 hours, 95% CI −13.17 to −4.03; 16 trials, 1137 participants; low-quality evidence), though there was substantial variability in the results. The need for intravenous hydration was generally low across trials, with fewer participants in the polymer-based ORS group requiring intravenous fluids (RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.57 to 0.98; 19 trials, 1877 participants; low-quality evidence). Subgroup analysis suggested that polymer-based ORS reduced the need for unscheduled intravenous fluids in participants infected with mixed pathogens (RR 0.63, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.96; 11 trials, 928 participants; low-quality evidence). However, no such effect was observed in participants with Vibrio cholerae infections (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.34; seven trials, 535 participants; low-quality evidence). There was no significant difference between the two types of ORS in the incidence of vomiting (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.14; 10 trials, 584 participants; very low-quality evidence), hyponatraemia (RR 1.82, 95% CI 0.52 to 6.44; four trials, 385 participants; very low-quality evidence), hypokalaemia (RR 1.29, 95% CI 0.74 to 2.25; two trials, 260 participants; low-quality evidence), or persistent diarrhoea (RR 1.28, 95% CI 0.68 to 2.41; two trials, 885 participants; very low-quality evidence). Authors' Conclusions: Polymer-based ORS demonstrated certain advantages over glucose-based ORS with osmolarity ≥ 310 mOsm/L. While comparisons with glucose-based ORS at ≤ 270 mOsm/L also favored polymer-based ORS, the analysis was underpowered to draw definitive conclusions.
